You are working in the SystemDNA repo, a React 18 + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind app in web/ that uses three, @react-three/fiber, @react-three/drei, @react-three/postprocessing, framer-motion and zustand. Build the public landing page at route "/" and move the existing 3D dashboard to "/city" using react-router-dom (install it). "/city?mode=replay" must open the dashboard in replay mode.
Open these existing files first for style and reuse: web/src/ui/theme.ts (colours), web/src/ui/AppShell.tsx, web/src/three/CityScene.tsx, web/src/store/useCityStore.ts (quality, reduceMotion).
Look: dark space background #05070d, neon accents (cyan #38bdf8, violet #a78bfa, red #ff3b5c, amber #ffb020, green #22e39a, pink #f472b6), glass cards (rgba(15,20,35,0.55), backdrop blur, 1px neon border), a display font for headings (Space Grotesk via Google Fonts) and a monospace font for code (JetBrains Mono).

PRODUCT FACTS (use this copy; do not invent numbers)
- Name: SystemDNA. Tagline: "Find References for your whole system, and fix them all."
- One-liner: SystemDNA shows what a code change will break across a whole system, then has a governed crew of IBM Bob agents fix every affected part and prove the change is complete.
- Problem: "Find references" only works inside one language. Real systems mix SQL, PySpark, Python, TypeScript, YAML and docs. Example: renaming orders.cust_id to customer_id can break a SQL transform and every model built on its alias customer_key, a PySpark job (including one that builds SQL from a string at runtime), the Python ORM model and API response schema, the TypeScript type and the React table that shows it, a revenue dashboard and the Finance month-end close that uses it, plus tests and docs. Today developers grep, ask teammates, fix one file at a time, and find the rest when a job fails.
- Why now: one AI agent works file by file; many agents at once are invisible and clash. Nobody can see or control what a swarm of agents is doing in the code.
- How it works (5 steps): 1 Map: scans a repo into a knowledge graph of every component across 7 layers (database, data pipelines, backend, API, frontend, dashboards, business processes). 2 Predict: pick one change, see the ripple: what breaks, how badly, in what order, which business process is hit. 3 Fix: parallel Bob agents fix every affected component in dependency order; each agent may only edit the files on its permit. 4 Govern and observe: the Agent City shows every agent live; city rules are enforced by Bob lifecycle hooks, not just drawn. 5 Prove: a re-scan shows 0 dangling references, tests pass, and the output is one PR, an impact report and a full audit trail.
- The 3 traps grep misses: Alias chain (stg_orders renames cust_id to customer_key, so downstream files never mention cust_id; found by SQL lineage). Dynamic SQL (export_job.py builds the query from a variable; found by a Bob Cartographer agent, medium confidence). Cross-language (a Python API field flows into a TypeScript type and a React table; found by the cross-layer linker).
- City laws: Permit law (edit only files on your permit), One builder per building, Traffic lights (a wave starts only when the wave above is green), Budget law (Bobcoin cap per agent and per change), Two-strike law (2 blocked actions = quarantine and rollback), Completeness law (done only when the re-scan shows 0 dangling references), Record law (every action is logged).
- Built with IBM Bob 2.0: Agent mode (fixer agents edit real files), Plan mode then hand-off to Agent, Parallel subagents (Cartographers per layer, fixers per node), Document understanding (reads the data dictionary PDF and ADR for owners and PII), Custom modes (Cartographer, Change Planner, Fixer, Inspector), Skills (propagate-rename fix recipes), Lifecycle hooks (PreToolUse blocks out-of-permit edits; SessionStart, PostToolUse and Stop stream events), MCP (SystemDNA tools get_impact, plan_change, start_wave, get_status, verify), Bob Shell (bob -p workers with --max-cost and --max-turns).
- Targets (label them "Target", never as achieved results): affected components found 100% of the known list (about 17 of 17); grep alone about half; time to find impact under 1 second; time to apply all fixes under 10 minutes; dangling references after the change 0; tests passing 100%; edits blocked outside a permit at least 1 shown live.
- Architecture: Bob IDE -> load balancer (HTTPS + WebSocket) -> one EC2 host running API + event server, MCP server, orchestrator, graph + impact engine, Bob workers + hooks -> DynamoDB (events, audit log), S3 (graph, replays), Secrets Manager, CloudWatch; the dashboard is a static site on CloudFront + S3.
- Event: IBM Bob 2.0 Hackathon on lablab.ai, 25-27 September 2026. Team of 6: 2 Cloud and Platform engineers, 4 Forward Deployed Engineers.

SECTIONS (web/src/landing/, one component per section)
1) Hero: full-screen R3F canvas with a slowly rotating DNA double helix made of glowing nodes; each base pair is coloured by one of the 7 layers and linked by thin light strands. Clicking anywhere sends a shockwave ripple through the helix (red, then amber, then grey). As the user scrolls, the helix unwinds and its nodes fly into a neural network, then settle into a small 3D city skyline (drive it from framer-motion useScroll progress into the scene). Overlay: "SystemDNA", the tagline, the one-liner, buttons "Enter Agent City" (-> /city) and "Watch the replay" (-> /city?mode=replay), and a small "Built with IBM Bob 2.0" text badge (text only, no logos).
2) Problem: "One rename. Seven layers." A vertical chain of glass cards for each thing the rename breaks, linked by a neural line that lights up as you scroll; a toggle "grep vs SystemDNA" dims the cards grep would miss and labels why.
3) How it works: the 5 steps as a scroll-driven timeline; a glowing synapse line fills between steps; each step has a small animated icon (Map: nodes connecting, Predict: ripple rings, Fix: worker dots moving in waves, Govern: a padlock and stop sign, Prove: a counter falling to 0).
4) Traps: three flip cards (front: trap name and a code snippet; back: why grep misses it and who finds it).
5) Agent City preview: a lazy-loaded mini 3D city loop (reuse CityScene with mock data if practical, otherwise a lightweight stand-in) where a ripple spreads and buildings turn green, with a legend of building and agent states.
6) Governance: the city laws as glowing badges; a short animation of a worker trying to step outside its permit and bouncing off a red barrier.
7) Built with IBM Bob 2.0: a responsive grid of the Bob features above with one line each.
8) Proof: the targets table styled as metric tiles labelled "Target"; read measured values from web/src/landing/metrics.ts where every value is null for now and a null shows "Measured live in the demo".
9) Architecture: an animated SVG diagram of the flow above with light dots travelling along the arrows.
10) Footer: event line, team line, a GitHub link whose URL comes from web/src/landing/siteConfig.ts (placeholder "#").

QUALITY RULES
- Smooth 60 fps: lazy-load the 3D hero and the city preview, cap particles, use instancing, no allocations inside useFrame; pause 3D when off screen.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion and the store's reduceMotion: no auto-rotation, no scroll morph (show the static skyline), no shockwave.
- Fallback: if WebGL is unavailable, show a static gradient hero with the same text and buttons.
- Responsive from 360 px phones to wide desktops; semantic headings (one h1); keyboard focus visible; alt text or aria-labels for visuals; colour is never the only signal.
- No tokens, keys, analytics or external scripts; only Google Fonts may load from outside.
- Tests (vitest + @testing-library/react): the landing page renders the h1 and tagline; "Enter Agent City" links to /city and "Watch the replay" to /city?mode=replay; metric tiles show "Target" and "Measured live in the demo" when values are null.
Run npx tsc --noEmit, npx vitest run and npm run build, fix every failure, then summarise the files you created.

# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# Mode Switching
